A target date is not a policy or a commitment; it is just noise. Bizarrely, at the same time, Britain will end up with the highest tax burden in our history. It is forecast to increase to 37.9% of GDP next year, and to continue to rise until 2031-32. Labour’s answer? You guessed it: more taxes. The Budget confirmed a new tax on the tourism industry. Only the bizarre mindset of a Labour Minister could believe that the way to help an industry is by imposing more taxes on it. As has often been said, “If socialists understood economics, they wouldn’t be socialists.” There are so many missed opportunities in the Budget. Retail, hospitality and leisure were crying out for support. As has been mentioned, we had proposals—which we would have been happy for the Labour party to copy—that would have taken 250,000 businesses out of paying business rates altogether, permanently. Labour’s solution was to take 70,000 businesses out temporarily, only giving back a fraction of what they had already taken away. This was a Budget of missed opportunities, and what alarms me most is the inability of Labour Members to recognise the damage they have already done, because that means they do not know how to get out of it. There is an alternative—a pro-business Conservative alternative—so bring on the election because we are looking forward to implementing that alternative at the earliest opportunity.

Items.AttributedTo: Olivia Bailey (Reading West and Mid Berkshire) (Lab)
Items.Value: I welcome the measures in the Budget that will give my constituents some much-needed breathing space as they look ahead to the winter. The £100 payment towards energy bills, the scrapping of gas standing charges and the extension of 0% VAT on electricity bills, will all make a difference to household budgets in my constituency at this pressured time. I also welcome measures to support small businesses, such as the fantastic Elysien that I visited last week, and our brilliant local pubs and brewers such as Renegade and Double-Barrelled. Today I wish to speak in my capacity as Chair of the Women and Equalities Committee, and because those facing discrimination and disadvantage are often the most exposed to financial pressures, I must start by saying that measures in the Budget to support people with the cost of living are particularly welcome. I also welcome the funding to tackle misogyny announced in the Budget, and the Government’s ambition in that area. In the Committee’s inquiry into the manosphere we have heard alarming evidence about online misogyny fuelling harm, and we have been left in no doubt that if we are to meet the Government’s ambition to halve violence against women and girls in a decade, we must urgently focus our attention, and our resources, on prevention. Although £15 million over three years is a welcome start, compare that with the vast profits being generated by the platforms and industries through which misogyny and hate are amplified. We are being outmatched, and as misogyny continues to plague our society, we must rise to the challenge. The Budget also contained some welcome measures for parents and carers. I welcome the changes to the carer’s allowance to remove the cliff edge. We cannot keep telling carers—the majority of whom are women—that we want them to participate in the workforce while maintaining a system that penalises them for trying to do so. I note that the changes will not be in force until 2030-31, and I would welcome additional commitments from the Government to support carers in the meantime. I also welcome the paid paternity leave for self-employed fathers and other parents announced in the Budget as an important first step towards the wider parental leave reform that we need. It is regrettable, however, that that gap in the system will not be filled until 2029. The Women and Equalities Committee has been clear that we need a pathway towards six weeks of paid paternity leave, and a simpler, fairer, more gender-equal parental leave system. The 18 months of the Government’s parental leave review will soon be up, and we hope and expect to see that pathway laid out. One of the biggest barriers to equal participation in the workforce remains access to affordable childcare, so I was a little disappointed that childcare measures were not included in the Budget this year. It is a huge achievement of this Government that we have overseen a record expansion of funded childcare—something I was proud to work on as a Minister. Too many lower-income parents are unable to access the support that they need to re-enter work or work longer hours. The Government already fund around 80% of childcare delivered in this country. We have in effect already created a new public service, and it is time that we reformed our complex system to reflect that reality, and to make universal childcare a centrepiece of the Government’s 10-year plan. These are not peripheral issues but fundamental barriers to economic growth. According to the Women’s Budget Group, women’s equal participation in the workforce could be worth £113 billion to our economy, even before we consider the enormous figures that could be unlocked by improving employment opportunities for disabled people and other groups who face barriers to work. That brings me to my final point. If we truly want to tackle inequality, we must have a conversation in this place about the barriers that prevent people from working, from earning, and from securing a better life for themselves and their families, and that means a proper conversation about welfare reform. The current system is both fiscally unsustainable and deeply unfair to the people it traps in a cycle of inactivity, so I am looking forward to the final reports of the Milburn review and the Timms review, and to the Government’s setting out concrete proposals in this area. I am also clear that in that necessary conversation about welfare reform, we must also talk about the wider barriers to employment, support for carers, the role of parental leave and, above all, access to universal childcare.

Britain needed a much bolder Budget for growth—one for families and businesses, and to boost our economy.

For families, heating—or even cooling—our homes, getting around and feeding the family are all costs that continue to rise. The energy price cap is set to rise again in January, and 1.4 million low-income households in higher council tax bands will miss out under this Budget. However, our Lib Dem essential energy guarantee would take £100 off the average bill for everyone, paid for by clawing back excess profits made by monopoly energy operators. We would also cut rail fares by 10%, bus fares to £1 and fuel duty by 10p, paid for by the Treasury’s fuel price windfall.

For most businesses, rent, rates, energy and hiring costs are going up. At DJ’s Play Zone in my local area, Mark says that his rates bill has gone up by 52%, from £21,000 to £32,000 a year, on top of the national insurance jobs tax and rising wages. He is running a small business in a big building, so small business relief never reaches him. The Chancellor’s new £18,000 threshold changes nothing for him and many other businesses that slip under the net.

My hon. Friend mentions the example of an indoor play centre where the business rates are going up. Is she concerned, as I am, that this winter those increases will simply price children out of play altogether?

Absolutely. That is why we need wholesale reform, looking at how we are supporting the businesses that need it and at the broken business rates system. Charlotte from Berkhamsted Bookshop tells me that the average independent bookshop will need to sell over 1,000 more books a year just to cover rising costs. Christopher, who runs a small martial arts academy in Tring, tells me that rising rent and service charges threaten his future, with almost no protection for small commercial tenants. Liberal Democrats have repeatedly called for more to be done to help our local businesses, including replacing business rates with a commercial landowner levy and cutting VAT on hospitality by 5p.

Does my hon. Friend agree with my constituent, Philippe Messy, who runs the excellent Little Wine Shop in Taunton, who was hoping to see a big move in VAT, but who has instead described the Budget as “a soufflé that did not rise—flat, flat, flat”?

I could not have put it better myself. On top of that there is the cost of hiring, as has been mentioned again and again. The Government have to tackle that for businesses.

If we truly want fresh hope for the future and for our wider economy, we need bold action. Supporting our entrepreneurs is key, and as Lib Dems who have pushed for a type of young entrepreneurs allowance for almost a decade, we are pleased to see that proposal and look forward to hearing more details. I would also push the Government to look at further work to support start-ups and scale-ups, including reviewing the seed enterprise investment scheme, tax on SEIS, tax credits and relief so that they work for businesses.

As for the founders’ relief, I ask the Government to work with the industry to ensure that it works. One founder said to me that they felt that if they stood on one leg and turned around enough times they might just about get close to getting some of it.

On incentivising innovation, the Government must take spin-outs from our world-leading universities across the UK more seriously. We are calling for the Government to quintuple proof-of-concept funding, create regional innovation centres and introduce standardised frameworks for negotiating intellectual property across the sector. As regards innovative spending, the extra £120 million for the Sovereign AI fund pales in comparison to the nearly £8 billion of active contracts with US tech giants or the billions spent on procurement. We call for a proper digital sovereign strategy to back our British businesses and to look at increasing research and development spending, so that we do not have to make decisions over Jodrell Bank, for example, and how that is impacting innovation.

Finally, we need a bold plan on Europe. We are calling for a growth and defence partnership with Europe, rejoining the single market and customs union. Not only can we cut taxes for families with that growth dividend, but inject real growth into our economy for families, businesses and our future.

Although the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade is no longer in his place, I start by thanking him and colleagues in the Department for the work they are doing with me and other local MPs in securing the long-term future of Jodrell Bank. I am proud that it is in my constituency and I am grateful for the work that he is doing. Like many colleagues, I welcome the Budget. Businesses need certainty and stability in order to invest, and I welcome the prudent and targeted decisions, particularly around the cost of living, which other hon. Members have touched on. Absorbing some costs in a moderate reduction in the fiscal headroom, as set out by the Chancellor, is sensible and creates the stability that helps to maintain, rather than undermine, business confidence. In recent months, Britain has proved extraordinarily resilient to the shocks caused by the conflict in the middle east—a war that, as other colleagues have pointed out, was recklessly supported by Conservative and Reform Members. Despite oil prices remaining above $100 a barrel, growth has been better than expected in Britain. Because of the stability from this Government and the measures provided in this Budget and in previous Budgets, there is now renewed hope for the future. That hope should be cause for optimism and provide a check on the constant doom and gloom that we often hear—a reminder that official forecasts are not destiny, but a target to beat. In the past year we have gone from the Leader of the Opposition saying we might need an IMF bailout, to the IMF saying that we have the best deficit reduction plan in the G7. In the past two years, we have consistently performed better than the forecasts. In March 2025, the OBR forecast 1% growth, but we grew 1.4%. In April this year, the IMF forecast 0.8% growth, but we hit 1.2% in the first half of the year alone. Even after upgrading its original forecast, it was still behind the curve. Forecasts are not destiny—optimism is warranted. Opposition parties sometimes seem almost to want Britain to need a bail-out—to will debt to rise, growth to slow or inflation to be higher—for their own narrow partisan self-interest, and to paint the worst possible picture. But we should be talking Britain up, not down. This is a great country to live, do business and invest in. I say clearly to hon. Members, particularly Conservative Members, believe in Britain or Britain will not believe in you. I welcome the pro-growth, pro-industrialisation policies in this Budget, particularly the plans to devolve power and funding so that Macclesfield, and every town, can invest in the things that matter to it—the plans to devolve business rates and empower local communities to benefit from the growth that they work hard to generate, and the devolution of income tax powers to follow in 2028. In Cheshire, we are very excited we are getting our first mayor in May. As Labour MPs in Cheshire, we have campaigned hard to get to this point. We want to replicate in our own area the tremendous journey that Manchester, Liverpool and other cities have had, so that we can unlock our potential. Fiscal devolution is an opportunity and a challenge: an opportunity to write our own destiny, and a challenge to say that if we invest in ourselves, back good growth projects and support innovation, industry and productivity, we can make ourselves richer without being reliant on Whitehall or the outside world. It is an opportunity that we in Cheshire and Macclesfield will seize with both hands. Breaking the link between Whitehall handouts and investment in Cheshire is a huge step towards our having more control over our future, and I support this Budget wholeheartedly.

Last Friday, I welcomed representatives from more than 40 local businesses to my business breakfast. The businesses were of different sizes and from different sectors, but they had the same clear message: the cost of doing business is too high. These are hard-working people. They want to be able to get on, do business, expand and invest in their staff, yet at every turn this Government make it harder.

Six in 10 small businesses feel that the Government are not on their side, according to a recent opinion poll. Higher employer national insurance contributions, increases in the minimum wage and soaring energy bills are squeezing margins, and we can add to that the mounting regulation and burdensome employment law introduced by this Government. Business confidence has been negative for seven consecutive months. Businesses needed a Budget that gave them confidence; instead, they were thrown a damp squib.

Perhaps we should not be surprised. This weekend, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, whom I respect, told us that she did not think that employers were working people. I invite her to Aldridge-Brownhills so that she can tell that to the people running our hair salons, restaurants, garages and delivery companies. Those are the people who are the first up in the morning to open up their business, leave last and often pay themselves last, after everyone else. That is the harsh reality. They do not stop being working people the moment that they give somebody else a job. That remark tells us exactly how little this Government understand the people who create jobs in our communities.

Items.AttributedTo: Sir Gavin Williamson (Stone, Great Wyrley and Penkridge) (Con)
Items.Value: My right hon. Friend raises the matter of extra regulation and extra tax. The people this Government are hurting and impacting on the most are young people, in terms of job opportunities. That certainly seems to be the case in my constituency. Is it the case in hers as well?

My right hon. Friend is absolutely spot on. I was just about to come to the impact on young people. Recruitment and training were also raised at my business breakfast. Local employers want to recruit, but finding people with the right skills and experience remains a challenge. Employers need a more flexible apprenticeship system that gives young people the skills and experience that local businesses are looking for. With almost 1 million young people outside education, employment or training, it is time to close the gap between the skills that employers need and the opportunities that young people can access. We need training that leads to real jobs, apprenticeships that work for employers and a welfare system that expects those who can work to do so. Ministers need to give businesses the confidence to recruit, yet the Government’s answer is always to spend more and tax more. Their decisions will have added £75.1 billion to the tax burden by the end of this Parliament, with taxes forecast to reach their highest level on record. Families and businesses across my constituency are being asked to pay for a Government who cannot live within their means. We cannot revive our high streets by taxing businesses out of business and into closing their doors. It is time that the Treasury assesses the cumulative impact of its tax increases and this Government’s policy choices on jobs and investment, before more livelihoods and more opportunities for the next generation are lost. The Prime Minister may like writing a blank cheque, but what he really needs is a reality check from businesses such as those in my constituency. Let me speak about a sector that is close to my heart—hospices. For families in Aldridge-Brownhills, hospices such as Acorns children’s hospice and St Giles hospice provide care, comfort and support at some of life’s most difficult moments. Their staff, volunteers and fundraisers make an extraordinary contribution, but charitable generosity cannot keep pace with rising costs indefinitely. As Hospice UK has made clear, this Budget failed to address the funding crisis, even as hospices are cutting frontline services. There is a crucial distinction between funding buildings and funding care. Capital investment is absolutely welcome, but a refurbished room cannot care for a child; we need the specialist nurses to staff it. When the NHS commissions care from a hospice, its contracts should reflect the cost of providing that care. Hospices need fair funding in all postcodes so they can retain staff and plan services with confidence. This Budget falls short. It may buy the Chancellor some breathing space, but it offers precious little to my constituents and local businesses. It ducks the difficult decisions, leaves the ballooning welfare bill unchecked and pushes today’s problems further down the road, leaving the country less prepared for tomorrow. Just yesterday, there was a U-turn on indefinite leave to remain, which will only increase the welfare bill. Was that costed in the Budget? I really would like to know. We have a Government who are more concerned with keeping their Back Benchers happy than with taking the tough decisions that this country needs. The Chancellor may have bought himself time, but it is my constituents who will pay the price.

I am pleased to be able to contribute to this Budget debate. I very much welcome the breathing space that this Budget provides for families across Merthyr Tydfil and Aberdare. I welcome the additional £450 million spending power delivered to the Welsh Government as a direct result of this Budget, which they will hopefully use to support public services across Wales. That builds on at least £6.5 billion of total additional spending power that has already been delivered to the Welsh Government over this spending review period as a result of decisions taken by this UK Labour Government. I am also pleased that this Labour Government are backing economic growth in Wales, delivering on our commitment on rail with £30 million to drive forward new stations in Wales, subject to the Plaid Cymru Government confirming that they will match our ambition. The Government are giving families in Wales breathing space through help with the things that matter most: energy costs, fuel, food prices, pensions and wages. Thanks to decisions taken by this Government, around 1 million households in Wales in council tax bands A to D will receive a £100 payment towards utilities. I am also pleased that tariffs have been removed on over 100 food products, helping with the weekly shop. Many of these are small things, but added together, they make a big difference to families across my constituency and across the country. Wales’s patron saint, St David, is famous for asking people to “do the little things”. The context is slightly different, but the principle is the same: taken together, little things can make a big difference. I also want to highlight the mineworkers’ pension scheme. I declare an interest, in that my brother is a former miner and many of my extended family have also worked in the coal industry. I will focus on the last remaining call, which is to transfer the guarantor’s fund. Many ex-miners were the lifeblood of the community in my part of Wales, not only building our communities but building and powering our country. Many sacrificed their life, and many more sacrificed their health—that was the real price of coal. We owe them a debt. The Labour party has made huge progress on the injustice of the mineworkers’ pension scheme since coming into government. We are the only party to take meaningful steps to put this right. In the 2024 Budget, the mineworkers’ pension scheme’s £1.5 billion investment reserve was transferred to its 110,000 members, resulting in a 32% pension bonus—around £29 a week. In the 2025 Budget, the British Coal staff superannuation scheme went through the same process, with its £2.3 billion investment reserve transferred to its 40,000 members. That resulted in a 41% pension bonus, or around £100 a week. I am pleased that in this Budget, the Chancellor announced that every penny of the surplus from the mineworkers’ pension scheme and the British Coal staff superannuation scheme will remain with those schemes and their members, rather than being divided with the Government. Crucially, the Chancellor also said that this is unfinished business, and committed to ensuring that the full transfer of the guarantor’s fund will follow. That will finally right this injustice, which miners have faced for too long. However, we need that final piece to be delivered sooner rather than later, for the sake of the many ex-miners who are elderly and the many who are in poor health. Many die every month. I recognise the urgency of this matter, and I pledge that I will continue to work with my colleagues. I say to former miners across my constituency: I will continue fighting for you until you get the justice you have been waiting so long for. Finally, although I welcome the freeze in fuel duty, I must again raise the scandal of local fuel prices. Fuel prices have remained stubbornly higher than in other areas, particularly in the Merthyr Tydfil part of my constituency. I have noted lower fuel prices in central London than in Merthyr Tydfil; even the Asda store in Merthyr Tydfil was charging around 10p per litre more than in any of its other local stores. When I met representatives of Asda earlier this year, they recognised this, and reduced their prices by 5p per litre within a few days, but the remaining retailers did not follow suit. While the war in Iran has made matters a whole lot worse, the impact in Merthyr Tydfil is worse than in many other local communities. Although I recognise that the Government cannot force retailers to lower their prices, I have contacted the Competition and Markets Authority to ask for its help in highlighting the unfairness of fuel prices in my community and their impact on my constituents, who feel that they are being unfairly ripped off at the fuel pumps. Building on this Budget, I ask the CMA to come to the table and see what it can do to help my constituents.

The Government have labelled today’s debate “fresh hope for the future”, but I regret that the Budget failed to meet the hopes of my constituents. My constituency contains a number of leading spin-out, innovation and engineering companies, from Oxford Ionics to Zero fuels and from the Jaguar and McLaren Formula E teams to Siemens Healthineers. They want to put the area on the map as one of the fastest-growing tech hubs in the country, yet too many face one major constraint: energy. The queue for grid connections faced by many new businesses and developments in my constituency goes far into the 2030s. Many households in the area are also used to power outages. The Cooper school in Bicester recently had to close for a day because of a lack of power. North West Bicester, a site for 6,000 homes, was delayed by more than two years purely because of a lack of grid connectivity. We now have two proposed mega data centres. Exeter college proposes a new centre south of Kidlington, while a large centre south-east of Bicester will require electricity equivalent to that needed for 1.4 million homes. That is a huge amount for an area already facing energy scarcity. My constituents are worried that the Chancellor’s commitment to pushing data centres to the front of the queue will overload local networks or delay connections for essential new services. The Government must commit to publishing an assessment of capacity before allowing data centres to jump the queue. I agree with the Prime Minister and Chancellor that we need to give more power back to the people and to end the UK’s excessive centralisation in London. In principle, I support the creation of a Thames valley mayor and regional devolution, but devolution must give local communities a stronger voice when it comes to the cumulative impact of development in our areas. New housing, data centres and major infrastructure projects cannot be considered in isolation. They make demands on the same roads, public services and electricity networks, and residents experience the combined impact. The pressure on roads, GP surgeries, schools and utilities must therefore be assessed across the whole area. Buried in the Budget document is another announcement of real interest to my constituents. There is £150 million of additional funds to support large asylum centres, such as that proposed for site A of MOD Bicester. My constituents and I oppose this scheme for many reasons, but in this Budget debate I will limit myself to the eye-watering costs of converting this derelict storage depot, which has never had accommodation for people, into a village for 1,256 asylum seekers. The best estimate is some £280 million in capital costs and £80 million in annual operating costs, which sums to more than £1 billion over 10 years. That raises serious questions about how far the additional £150 million will stretch. I urge the Chancellor, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury and their officials to take a close look at Home Office spending. I fear that they will find once again that the asylum programme is out of control. They will certainly find that building new accommodation at MOD Bicester is a bad deal for the taxpayer. Turning to hospitality, pubs, cafés and restaurants are key to the health of the high streets of Bicester, Kidlington and Woodstock. In the rural villages of my constituency, the local pub, alongside the church and the primary school, is the key local institution. Too many such businesses, including the much-loved Fat Zebra café in Bicester’s Market Square, have been forced to close. Too many others tell me that they are facing mounting and unrelenting cost rises. The changes on business rates relief are welcome, but businesses tell me that they may not be enough to keep them afloat. I urge the Treasury to look again at the Liberal Democrat proposal to cut VAT for hospitality businesses. This Budget was a missed opportunity for my constituents. It failed to assure them that infrastructure would come first, before major developments. It backed a failing Home Office programme for large asylum centres. It failed to deliver a stronger local voice, despite promises of devolution, and it failed to support the pubs, cafés and restaurants at the heart of our communities. I urge the Government to give my constituents more hope in the future.

It is lovely to be back speaking in the Chamber in a debate on a welcome Budget for the life sciences. If you will indulge me, Madam Deputy Speaker, I would like to put on my pharmacy hat and geek out a bit about the life sciences announcements in this Budget. We have more than £1 billion of private investment in the sector, backed by nearly £70 million of Government funding, supporting 1,000 jobs. We have £500 million in a new research hub in Manchester for Convatec, which makes stoma care products. We have £300 million in a research facility in Oxfordshire for Vertex. We have £200 million in Loughborough for manufacturing respiratory medicines, including the new generation of inhalers. Closer to home, just yesterday Ministers announced £21 million for the west midlands clinical commercial catalyst, with Coventry University among the partners. That is investment in British research, in manufacturing, and in skilled people who work in both sectors. I also welcome the Chancellor’s decision to remove VAT on orphan drugs—rare disease treatments—providing direct care for compassionate use and early access schemes. That will make it easier for people to access new treatments and continue their care. However, access is not only about the newest treatments; it is also about people’s ability to get the medicines on which they already depend. We heard recently that Europe’s last fully integrated medicine factory, in Austria, is considering closing down, due to Chinese competition. That should make us think carefully about where our medicines come from, because in Britain we rely heavily on medicines and active ingredients from India and China. With tariffs returning and global supply chains becoming increasingly uncertain, we cannot afford to depend on a handful of countries or factories for medicines that patients simply cannot afford. We have seen supply problems with Creon, the pancreatic enzyme treatment used by people with cystic fibrosis and pancreatic cancer; with particular formulations of sodium valproate, lamotrigine and phenobarbital, medicines used to treat epilepsy; and with ramipril, a common drug used by millions of people to treat high blood pressure and heart conditions. As any pharmacist knows, missed treatments can have an impact on health, and can mean that a condition being managed at home ends in an emergency admission. That is worse for patients, and it costs the NHS more. Although I applaud the work that the DWP is doing to help more people with health conditions into work—and I look forward to the Milburn review—if someone with epilepsy cannot reliably get their anti-seizure medication, how can we expect them to work, let alone to be productive? If someone cannot get the medicine they use to keep a heart condition stable, and as a result they become too unwell to work, how can we talk about improving Britain’s productivity? Ensuring that people can manage their health conditions, stay in work and contribute to our economy must be part of that conversation as well. I welcome the Government’s £520 million life sciences innovative manufacturing fund and the Chancellor’s additional £20.4 billion of financial capacity for the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank. The Government have made a strong start in attracting investment, but we also need to be strategic and proactive about where that investment goes. I therefore ask Treasury Ministers, Health Ministers and Business Ministers to work together to establish which essential medicines and ingredients are more critical, where our supply chains are most vulnerable, and where manufacturing in Britain can make the biggest difference. Let us then use some of that finance to attract private investment and build up our manufacturing capacity before the next shortage becomes a crisis. We have excellent scientists and researchers; let us make sure that we have the capacity to make and reliably supply the medicines on which patients depend. Finally, I want to say a little about what the Budget means for my constituents. More than 40,000 local people are set to benefit from the £100 payment towards their energy bills this winter, and that help is very welcome. For those working in our shops, pubs and care homes, the increase in the national living wage to £13.21 next April will mean more money in their pockets. I particularly welcome the additional business rate relief for our high streets, supporting the independent shops, cafés and pubs that are so important to our communities, along with the removal of the relief from vape shops. Our high streets are about more than shopping; they are places where neighbours meet, where local people make a living, and where we take pride in our communities.

Some have dubbed this a “steady as she goes” Budget. That has been interpreted differently by those on different sides of the debate: some have taken it as praise while others have taken it as a criticism. You might be surprised to hear, Madam Deputy Speaker, that I fall on the side of that being a criticism. That is because I hold the really controversial view that avoiding market turmoil is a minimum requirement for a Budget; it is necessary but not sufficient, especially given the challenges we face in this country. I accept that we face constraints, given the war in Iran and everything that is doing to the country’s finances, inflation, energy prices and so on, but we have more challenges to face up to. This Government actually recognise those challenges. They have commissioned reports on welfare reform, but they have pushed it to the other side of the Budget. They have a Chancellor who recognises that we need a plan to spend 3% of GDP on defence, but those decisions, too, have been pushed further down the track. They understand that growth has been appalling in this country for a long time, yet they have not revealed what their plan for growth will be. These are all known issues that are unaddressed in this Budget, and I think that is a massive missed opportunity. That is not for want of measures in this Budget. There are a record-breaking 98 measures in the Budget, but they add up to the lowest total value we have seen for a very long time. Let us get into some of those. The Government have praised themselves for their £100 energy support package, and who can be churlish about £100 in times like these? But the truth is that the scheme is insufficient and poorly targeted. The tragedy is that we had an energy crisis in 2022, when we had to deliver huge sums of money, almost universally. Everybody said, “We cannot let this happen again; we must have a much more targeted scheme in future.” Four years on, what is the system we have? We are relying on the valuations of properties from 1991 to target our support. What a failure of Government. Moreover, hundreds of thousands of low-income households are now set to miss out on support, and those most in need of support will not get enough. Looking at all the “breathing space” measures combined, those in the very poorest deciles will get, on average, just £15 more than all the others. This Government could have done far more to deliver on breathing space. For instance, they could have looked to the Liberal Democrat proposal for an essential energy guarantee, which would be more targeted and would provide more support at the right income levels. This has been a real failure of Government. A second measure for which the Government have been praising themselves is the bank tax and the contributions that they have got that sector to make. We called for a bank tax and so we broadly welcome it, but why did they not go further? The banking industry expected this measure to be permanent and expected it to be set at 8%, and bank shares went up when we found out that that was not what the Government were going to do. In the Treasury Committee this morning, we heard from people in the banking sector, who said that they did not believe the tax would affect competitiveness and that they would be unlikely to pass on the costs to the consumer. Basically, the banks have been getting £1 billion a week this year because mortgage rates and interest rates are so high. They could have been squeezed some more, and this Government failed to do it. On living standards, this morning the Resolution Foundation described the situation as “catastrophic”. The 2010s was the worst decade on record, with 14% growth in real household disposable income. For the 2020s, the OBR’s growth forecast is 1.4%. This is a tragedy for every working family in Britain, and that is before we get on to the cost of doing business or the spending pressures that are pencilled in for down the track. Courtrooms, classrooms and councils are all set for real-terms cuts under this Government—it is all in black and white. That is their proposal to come. All of this can be solved in only one way: via growth. I said at the beginning of my speech that there is a lack of a growth plan, but there is one waiting on the table for the Government. We would like the Prime Minister to stop having an open, frank conversation with himself on Europe, and to actually start putting forward some concrete proposals such as rejoining the single market. That is the quickest single measure to boost growth in this country, and we should get on with it. This Budget has deferred decisions on welfare, defence, Europe, public services and growth. The Prime Minister came into office promising to end 40 years of neoliberalism, but it will surely make its 41st birthday. It has been a missed opportunity that the Government will come to regret. Budgets do not come around very often—just ask any of the six Chancellors in the last six years. Political capital is a depreciating asset—it is best to spend it early, and the Government have utterly failed to do so.

The theme of today’s Budget debate is “fresh hope for the future”, so I would like to take the opportunity to review the pledges that I made to my constituents at the general election, how this Budget helps to deliver on them and, given that the Government have said we are at the start of the process, my fresh hopes for the future. But since Opposition Members are so interested in getting into a conversation, I will deal with them first. Last Wednesday, my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer set out a Budget that is the best-received Labour Budget in 23 years. That has been indicated very clearly, because the public and the markets have accepted it as a fantastic development. You can hear the disappointment from Opposition Members. You can hear that they are desperate for their attack lines, which are not getting through, in order to get public attention back on them, but what have we actually heard? From the Opposition Front Bench we heard about £30 billion of unfunded tax cuts. That is what the Conservatives’ plan is so far. On their own figures, the figure is £30 billion so far, but that is exactly what happened with the Liz Truss mini-Budget. They have learned no lessons from exactly that economic situation in what they put to us today. I promised my constituents that we would have a thriving local economy and support for the town centre, and Crawley’s economy is thriving. Anyone looking at it would have to accept that. Our major employers in the area are expanding. Developments such as the Government-funded Crawley Innovation Centre are bringing forward the new generation of technologies that will generate further economic growth in this country. Business rate changes are making it easier for properties on the high street. Many of the reforms set out in the Budget are going to make things considerably easier for people. High street rental auctions will enable us to tackle people who own property but, for their own financial reasons, are not putting people in. My hope for the future is that we can get further rate reform, and start addressing the unfair practices in the delivery industry that are allowing that sector and online retailers to kill off many of our high street businesses. My second pledge is to have housing that delivers for local people. We have the first-time buyer scheme—“Your First Home”—and first-time buyer ISAs. We have planning reforms coming through. We have £432 million for ending rough sleeping. We have over £40 billion for the biggest investment in affordable housing in a generation. We have new towns, and greater rights for private tenants through the Renters’ Rights Act 2025. We are delivering for people on housing. My hope for the future is more funding for affordable housing, moving away from the current financial structures, direct delivery from the Government, an end to hope value and housing revenue account reform. I have said that I want a better future for Crawley’s children, and what do we have? We have paid maternity leave so that fathers can spend the first critical weeks with their children, and more fathers can set the tone for their relationship to develop. We have the expansion of 30 hours of free childcare and SEND reform coming forward. We have the return of Sure Start—I do not know why it has new branding—in our communities. We have an end to the two-child poverty trap, which Opposition Members begged us not to remove. We have the expansion of free school meals, and the fastest reduction in poverty of any first-term Government in this country’s history. My hope for the future is that we continue to work towards ending child poverty, with action on those not in employment, education or training, ensuring every SEND child gets the support they need and creating real social mobility. I pledged real action on crime and antisocial behaviour, and we have the neighbourhood policing guarantee, an end to the £200 threshold for shoplifting, and new offences, including respect orders to ban repeat offenders from public places. We have preventive departmental spending, so we can really put in place the action necessary to protect our communities. My hope for the future is that we take the gloves off the police, bring in judicial reform to make it easier to send criminals to jail, make better use of automated technology and make greater use of on-the-spot penalties. Lastly, on a better resourced NHS that is there when people need it, we have the NHS 10-year plan and national plans for diseases such as cancer, rapid action on waiting lists, new capital investment, a huge expansion of diagnostic equipment and record investment in our national health service. My hope for the future is that the service focuses on keeping people well, rather than addressing their needs only when they are sick, and that we move services back into every postcode, where possible. There should be no limits on the aspiration of this Government or those of our constituents for our country. We should look at the progress that has already been made on the ills that affect our society. This Budget is taking us another step closer to the future that we all seek, and I look forward to many more Budgets from my right hon. Friend the Chancellor of the Exchequer.

This Budget might be described as the “John Lennon Budget”—it expects us to imagine a better future. Actually, the Chancellor’s performance was more like a better Lennon lyric:

“Life is what happens to you

While you’re busy making other plans”,

because this Budget was long on platitudinous plans and short on decisive delivery. Leaving aside the self-evident exponential crisis of welfare spending—I say self-evident, but perhaps I should explain that benefits are due to hit £431 billion—there are three macroeconomic weaknesses in the Budget, which I will seek briefly to highlight.

The Prime Minister may say that he has to wait for the Milburn and Timms reviews, but while he is doing so and those plans are being hatched, 13.5% of all young people in the UK were not in education, employment or training in January to March this year. One million people aged 16 to 24 are without a job, training or education. To echo the comments of the hon. Member for Widnes and Halewood (Derek Twigg), this is a waste of talent on a scale that is a national scandal. The Budget represented a wasted opportunity to address those issues and, in particular, to build the skills that might enable those people to gain a necessary job. The failure to address that may become the defining characteristic of this Administration.

These are not new problems. I was the Skills Minister, as some people in the Chamber will know. I was well aware of the root causes of NEETs and how we might address them. We managed to reduce the number that we inherited in 2010 by almost 300,000 by 2015, and I was also able also to build up the number of apprenticeships to the greatest number in modern times: over 500,000. Since then, that number has dwindled. It is only by equipping people with skills that have economic value—skills that allow them to the best they can be—that we can also sustain an economy which is desperate for those skills.

What successive Governments have done instead is to import labour. Every time we import labour and every time we make it easier to do so, we displace the investment in our own workforce, both in the young people I described and in the existing workers who need to be reskilled or upskilled. The myth was perpetuated, largely by the Treasury—
Will my right hon. Friend give way?
I am always happy to give way to my right hon. and learned Friend.

My right hon. Friend is making a very powerful speech. Does he share my disappointment and dismay with this fact—that, for every young Brit who is hired today, 27 young foreign workers are hired? Young people are being locked out of the labour market because of mass immigration.

My right hon. and learned Friend is absolutely right. Young people are being forced to compete with those foreign workers for a scarce number of jobs. The only people who support that policy are dim-witted bourgeoise liberals and hard-hearted plutocrats, because both of them glory in the idea of foreign labour. That foreign labour is edging Britons out of jobs and, by so doing, weakening our economy.
On that point, will the right hon. Gentleman give way?
I happily give way.

The right hon. Gentleman surely has not missed the evidence that, since his party’s botched Brexit deal, it has become more expensive to do business in the UK, businesses are wrapped up in red tape, and many businesses have moved abroad, taking good, high-quality jobs with them. We have a NEETs crisis in this country, caused by many different factors. One of the reasons that there are graduates who cannot get jobs is because his party’s ridiculous Brexit deal has driven businesses abroad. If we get back into the single market and make doing business cheaper, those businesses will come back here and create jobs for British young people.

I was going to address the issue of trade later, but the hon. Lady has encouraged me to do so now. The truth is that the balance of payments has been a neglected subject in this Parliament and for successive Governments for decades. We never sold as much to Europe as Europe sold to us, and that balance was out of kilter for the whole time that we were members of the European Union.
On that point, will the right hon. Gentleman give way?

No, I will not give way again, because there is only so much you can teach the Liberal Democrats!

The balance of trade figures was once a pivotal announcement in Parliament and for Governments. That has been forgotten as we have chosen to import more and more goods into this country, and to make fewer and fewer. The hon. Lady will recognise that, given that I represent a rural constituency that grows a lot of the food we consume, I am particularly sensitive to the fact that we have made ourselves dependent on foreign food imports. That is preposterous. We need to shorten supply chains and make ourselves more economically resilient. As the Prime Minister said, actually—
On that point, will the right hon. Gentleman give way?

I was about to make a point, but I will then give way once more to see whether I can teach the hon. Lady something more. As the Prime Minister said, we must remanufacture—we must build our manufacturing capacity again. Successive Governments have failed to do this. I do not claim any credit for any political party, and I certainly claim no credit for the Liberal Democrats.

The right hon. Gentleman is absolutely contradicting himself. He has simultaneously said that we need to shorten supply chains to improve our food security while defending the very trade barriers that prevent British importers and exporters from getting food to each other on a shorter supply chain. It was the right hon. Gentleman’s party that agreed the terrible trade deals with New Zealand and Australia that have put up food prices and undermined British farmers. Would he like to apologise for that? After 10 years, we are still teaching the Conservatives how damaging their trade deals were.

I mentioned my record on apprenticeships. I was in the coalition Government when I was able to bring about that outcome, with the full support of Liberal Democrat Ministers. It was Vince Cable, actually, as Secretary of State, who understood the need to build skills and train domestic workers so that we were not dependent, in the way that I described, on European goods or goods from anywhere else in the world. We just need to make more of what we consume. It is not hard to work out.

I said that I would deal with one or two other things, and time is pressing. Productivity is a macroeconomic problem that has faced all Governments. Declining productivity over time means that we spend a great deal of money on things from which we do not get a great deal of outcome. Our productivity is worse than some of our key competitors. The Government need to focus on that; the previous Prime Minister and his Ministers said that they would, but there was little about that in the Budget.

To summarise, I think it was Disraeli who said, “Men are not the victim of circumstances; they create circumstances.” It is not enough to blame context for the failure to address the macroeconomic problems of skills, productivity and immigration. More must be done, and done soon.

This past weekend, out on the doorstep speaking to constituents in Clwyd North, I was reminded once again that the issues that people care about most are often very different from the arguments that dominate social media. Away from the toxicity and division that can sometimes fill our feeds, people were not so interested in political point scoring. Instead, they wanted to talk about the practical challenges they face every day: paying their bills, accessing healthcare, supporting their families and making their money go a little further. The message I heard time and again was that people can see that this Budget is responding to those everyday pressures, despite global challenges. They welcome measures that will help with the cost of living, whether that is support with rising bills or action to bring down the cost of everyday items in their shopping baskets. These may be small changes in isolation, but when people are balancing a household budget every month, small savings can make a big difference. They welcome the £100 payment towards energy bills and the extension of the 0% VAT rate on electricity bills. They welcome the removal of the gas standing charge, too. This change, which has long been called for, will mean that households pay only for the gas they actually use; for too long, households have paid unavoidable fixed costs regardless of how much energy they use. This is a welcome step, but I want to see real progress on electricity standing charges, too. Many families in north Wales are rightly frustrated that they pay some of the highest standing charges in the country—paying before they have even switched on a light. We have heard the Chancellor make it clear that removing the standing charge for electricity is the next area of focus, and I will be pressing for that commitment to be delivered so that my north Wales constituents have a fair deal. Of course, I heard local people talk about public services. I heard concerns about waiting lists, access to healthcare, and support for additional learning needs in our schools. No one pretends that money alone will solve those challenges, but extra investment will give us a far better chance of tackling them. I therefore welcome the extra £450 million of additional funding coming to Wales, which builds on the largest funding settlement since devolution, delivered in the spending review by this Labour Government. My constituents want to see shorter waiting lists, better support for children and stronger public services. They want to see funding translated into results. It will be up to the minority Plaid Cymru Government in Wales to make that happen by getting on with the day job, with fewer consultations and more action. Finally, one thing that genuinely encouraged me on the doorstep was a sense that people were starting to see politics as more connected to their everyday lives. There was support for our new Prime Minister, with one constituent saying, “I could imagine the Prime Minister standing on my doorstep having this very conversation.” That comment stayed with me, because it was not just about the Prime Minister; it was about feeling heard. People want politicians who speak their language, who understand the pressures facing them and who are focused on the issues that matter to them most. This Budget responds to many of the concerns that people have raised with me in person, while providing welcome additional investment and opportunity for Wales. I will continue working to ensure that the people of Clwyd North see the full benefit of that investment.

Last Wednesday my constituents in Eastleigh looked to the Chancellor for real help with the cost of living. While some of the measures that he announced are welcome, I am afraid that this Budget lacks ambition, and is short term and poorly targeted. According to the Resolution Foundation, the one-off household energy payment based on council tax band rather than need means that 1.4 million low-income households in higher bands will miss out, while the scrapping of gas standing charges will save the typical household just £1.83 a month. The cuts to VAT on electricity and fuel duty both end next July, long before the OBR expects pressure on family budgets to ease. For constituents like Susan, a widow who lives in a park home in Fair Oak, the Budget offered very little. She is off the main gas grid and has no choice but to heat her home with liquid petroleum gas, which is far more expensive and is not protected by the energy price cap. Her £100 payment will barely touch the sides, and scrapping standing charges does nothing for her. Will the Minister set out what support the Government will provide for off-grid households like Susan’s, who rely on liquid petroleum gas and are not protected by the energy price cap? The Chancellor’s decision to raise the threshold for small business rates relief from £12,000 to £18,000 is welcome. However, the policy does not live up to the headline, benefiting only a limited number of businesses in Eastleigh. On Thursday, I hosted a post-Budget business breakfast in my constituency. Lucy, who runs Telmar CNC, a precision engineering firm in Chandler’s Ford, told me that her rates bill has doubled in six years, and manufacturers like her business got nothing. Jane runs Elite Hair Salon, which, as a microbusiness, is too small for the changes to make any difference. She told me, “Overall, this Budget has done little to support my business or many others within the hair and beauty sector.” I welcome the extra small producer relief. However, raising alcohol duty yet again in February will hit the very pubs and drinkers that small brewers depend on, and that is why we oppose it. We are approaching Remembrance Sunday; and, in the current climate, ensuring that our armed forces are properly equipped is more urgent than ever. In Eastleigh, Stuart, who runs GW Martin & Co, has welcomed the Government’s commitment to small firms in the defence investment plan, but he told me, “We would like to see greater urgency in funding this necessary investment as we have capacity and capability to respond quickly, which will create jobs, growth and revenue.” Instead, the plan to reach 3% of GDP on defence has been pushed back to next year’s spending review. James, who owns JLMS—an apprenticeship provider—told me, “This was not a Budget for youth employment.” The payment for taking on an apprentice has not gone up in five years, while the cost of employing and training a young person keeps rising. The Chancellor had a choice. He could have reversed the increase to employer national insurance contributions, which has sent job vacancies to a five-year low. Instead, he told young people to wait for another review. On plan 2 student loans, this Budget was again silent. It was an opportunity to reverse last autumn’s deeply unfair decision to freeze the repayment threshold from April 2027 for three years. With the minimum wage rising and the threshold frozen, we are approaching the point where a graduate on the minimum wage could have to start repaying. I urge the Treasury to scrap the freeze and link the threshold to average earnings. I am pleased that the Chancellor has finally listened to Lib Dem calls to scrap the carer’s allowance cliff edge. That is a welcome first step, but it will not come into force until 2030, and carers trying to balance work with looking after a loved one need this safety net now, not in four years. Will the Minister commit to bringing forward its introduction so that carers do not have to wait until 2030? Eastleigh needed a Budget with real ambition, but this one falls short. I urge the Chancellor to go further.

I am glad to support this excellent Budget. I welcome and agree with the Chancellor’s praise for his predecessor, my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves), whose commitment to secure economic foundations has helped to fund sustained public investment and deliver growth. It has helped the Chancellor rightly to offer breathing space now and fresh hope for the future. I will focus on the latter, but, on breathing space, the Budget delivered, with 41,760 households in my constituency receiving the £100 household energy payment. As someone whose professional career was in the private sector, I was particularly delighted to see the two-year business rate freeze, which will benefit 336 local retail, hospitality and leisure properties in Rugby, Bulkington and the villages. There was much in the Budget, too, on fresh hope for the future. The words of the Prime Minister are important in this context. In his Labour conference speech, he said: “Hope comes from honesty…It comes from saying the things politicians usually avoid.” It is what I call hard-headed hope. We need what I call the responsibility revolution: a focus on what each of us as individuals or organisations should contribute—or indeed sacrifice—rather than on what entitlements we are to receive. We older folk have a responsibility to the next generation, so my speech will focus primarily on the physical embodiment of fresh hope for the future: our young people. There can be no more important long-term issue than their interests. In addressing a long-term challenge for those at the opposite end of the age spectrum, the Prime Minister set out in his Labour conference speech how the Government will adjust the pension triple lock, which is a bold and much-needed move. He also said that “we will need to show the same boldness for our young people, too.” The Budget did that in several ways. I warmly welcome my right hon. Friend the Chancellor’s announcements of the Your First Home equity loan scheme and the first-time buyer ISA. That young people are priced out of affordable housing is a national scandal. Thousands of people in my constituency will also appreciate the much-needed 3.9% increase in the national living and minimum wage. The young entrepreneurs allowance is a vital pro-young people, pro-entrepreneurship measure. Let us encourage young people across the country to consider entrepreneurship as a viable career option. However, we need to go much further to provide hope for the future. We need to keep going until we can truly say that our young people are equipped sufficiently to be the architects of the future rather than tenants in a world designed by the older generation and all too often shaped by their interests. I would like to see the appointment of a Minister for younger and future generations sitting in Cabinet to scrutinise existing and future policy and legislation through the lens of how it benefits the next generation. We also need an independent body to hold the Government’s feet to the fire, so how about an office for intergenerational fairness? Last year, I coined the phrase “youth triple lock” because I wanted to focus attention on young people’s needs and the need for some rebalancing. I suggest an above-inflation increase in the student maintenance loan. The Prime Minister hinted at that in a social media post with the Chancellor when he said that student loans are “one to come back to.” I also suggest free bus passes and something on housing, which, as I stated earlier, was covered extensively by the Chancellor’s excellent Budget. There remains a risk that the social contract with our young people is fraying, so let us show that our Labour Government are not slowing down but accelerating our efforts to empower young people. Our role is not just doing what will make us popular with a plurality of mainly older voters; we need to rebalance things, because investing more in our young people is in the best interests of our economy as they are the innovators, the entrepreneurs, the workers, the business owners, the public servants and much more of tomorrow. We must unleash their potential. More importantly, it is the moral thing to do; it is the fair thing to do; it is the Labour thing to do. I commend the Budget for all its measures, and in particular those regarding young people. As ever, measures to empower young people are a down payment on the future and, as with all healthy investments, regular, judicious and generous investment pays dividends in the long run. I hope that the 10-year plan will be another opportunity to demonstrate that to the younger generation.

Given the time constraints, I will keep my remarks as short as possible. Although there are things that are welcome in this Budget , such as business rate relief and energy cost relief, it does not meet the challenges my constituents in Yeovil are facing, let alone pave the way for the biggest change in a generation that this Government keep saying they are going to deliver.

For a start, rural communities have been completely overlooked again. The £100 off most people’s energy costs is great, but it is not means-tested, and is matched to a broken council tax system. For us in rural Somerset, the biggest issue is the price of heating oil, which has doubled in the last year. What we needed was an urgent price cap— I have spoken to residents who have said they are not heating their homes because they cannot afford heating oil. That is unfair, and the Government need to provide real help.

There was nothing in the Budget for farmers, the backbone of our rural economy. That adds insult to injury, given Labour has increased taxes on farmers, while cutting the farming budget in England by a further £100 million and locking farmers out of funding by running applications for the sustainable farming incentive as if they were selling Glastonbury tickets—believe me, I know how hard they are to get. That is not just bad for Somerset’s economy; it threatens our food security at exactly the time we need to be strengthening it. That is why we Liberal Democrats have called for the farming budget to be increased by £1 billion a year.

More broadly, by missing many of the big-picture challenges, the Budget has failed my Yeovil constituency.

My hon. Friend is making an excellent case for rural communities on heating oil, farming and other issues, but may I add the failure of this Government to extend the rural fuel duty scheme? My rural North Cornwall constituency does not have buses running to hospitals, educational opportunities and jobs. Does he agree that the Government missed an opportunity to extend that scheme to help our rural constituents?

I agree with my hon. Friend. One of the biggest issues we have in Somerset is that even if there is a bus, sometimes it is so delayed, it is four hours late and students cannot get to college.

The can has been kicked down the road to the spending review next year as to how the Government plan to meet their NATO commitment of spending 3.5% of GDP on defence. Yet again, that leaves many of the cutting-edge defence firms that are the beating heart of Yeovil’s economy in uncertain times. Similarly, there was nothing in the Chancellor’s speech on education, when 70% of schools across England have had less funding in real terms than in 2010 and we have a growing SEND funding black hole. Investment in education is an investment in the future of this country and a sure-fire way to drive growth, so it is disappointing to see that funding solutions to this issue have also been kicked down the road.

One of the biggest issues impacting growth is how we do taxation. Business relief is great, but I do not know how many more of us have to call it “the broken business rates system” before the message gets through. So many businesses have contacted me since the Budget saying, “It is great, you have helped some, but you have not helped us. We are at the point of closing our doors.” Business rates need abolishing and replacing with a commercial landowner levy.

That is not all, however. Council tax is one of the biggest challenges raised by Yeovil constituents, because the system is out of date and we need bold Government action to change that. Unfortunately, the Government have decided not to rise to those challenges in this Budget and the people of Yeovil will continue to suffer the consequences of this Government’s inaction.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker, for the opportunity to contribute to the final day of the Budget debate. It is a Budget that this Government can be proud of, a Labour Budget, a Budget that will deliver fresh hope for the future, and a Budget that will put £100 back into the pockets of 44,430 households in Dagenham and Rainham. Though the council tax rebate of £100 to help with energy bills might not sound like much, with the energy bills breathing space scheme, coupled with the Government’s other measures, such as no VAT on electricity till July ’27, the abolishing of standing charges on gas bills and capping new levies on energy bills at 0% until 2030, we are taking action to reduce household energy debt in every postcode. With such a focus on making utilities affordable, I cannot help but feel hopeful that the failing water companies who extort us for resources will one day be brought back into public ownership, finally ending the race to the bottom that Thatcherism started, where profit margins and shareholder bonuses are put above quality of service and the people that rely on it. Speaking of services and the fresh hope that last week’s Budget set out, I wholeheartedly welcome the move to finally open up Stratford International, providing Eurostar access in east London. I have no doubt that this investment will provide a much-needed boost to the local economies in some of the most deprived areas of the capital. While that gives my constituents easier access to Europe, those living at Beam Park in the south of my constituency are still waiting for the train to Fenchurch Street. In fact, those residents are still waiting for the train station, which was promised to new homeowners and renters by the last Conservative Government, only for the plug to be pulled and promises to be broken. My helpful suggestion is that perhaps we should ask the last Government to own that decision. Despite the absence of an announcement that would deliver for Beam Park, I remain tenacious in my pursuit of the vital infrastructure that my constituents in Dagenham and Rainham were promised, and I very much hope, given the renewed focus on transport in London, that the £13.9 million shortfall to deliver this station can be found. While my campaign for Beam Park station continues, my campaign to deliver a new and expanded emergency department for the Queen’s hospital in Romford, which serves my constituents, has been won, thanks to this Labour Government. We campaigned for £35 million and this Labour Government, ahead of their landmark Budget, awarded the Barking, Havering and Redbridge trust £42 million to redesign the accident and emergency unit at Queen’s hospital. The party that built the NHS is now ending corridor care and delivering an NHS that is fit for the future. On the subject of health, it would be remiss of me not to mention environmental health, not least because of the Rainham volcano, a burning historic landfill that blights the health of the community in part of my constituency. Given the sheer scale of historic landfills in the country, I was disappointed not to see reinvestment in the Environment Agency to help these problems, but I am hopeful that, as the Government transform Britain, I can continue ticking off my pledges from 2024. If any Ministers are listening, I have covered my wish list in this contribution. As the Member of Parliament for a working-class constituency often described as London’s red wall, I was overjoyed to hear the Chancellor unveil plans to deliver paid paternity leave for self-employed workers. I am honoured to serve under my hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) as deputy chair of the all-party parliamentary group for tradespeople, and I know that this policy will give fresh hope to the plumbers, electricians, brickies and other tradesmen who will benefit from paid paternity leave from April 2029, giving self-employed dads the opportunity to be at the start of family life when it matters most. This is a real win for the work of the APPG, and it will make a tangible difference to family lives in Dagenham and Rainham, which is home to thousands of tradespeople and small business owners. I will bring my contribution to a close very simply, as I started. This was a Budget the Government can be proud of: a Labour Budget that delivers respite for today and fresh hope for the future.

I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, as a former county councillor. It is safe to say that I have not been inundated with emails praising this Budget or crediting it for tackling the thorny issues that my constituents face. Those eligible will welcome the £100 energy bill payment going towards their soaring bills, but the more than 10,000 of my constituents reliant on heating oil will wonder where they are going to find the rest of what has often been a £500 price hike on their oil bills. They will also be asking why the Government have cut VAT for those who rely solely on electricity but are happy to rake in double the VAT receipts from others who face those soaring bills. Removing VAT on those bills would put another £50 back in the pockets of those who have to fill a 1,000 litre tank. The Government are benefiting from a VAT windfall, and it is time that they gave that back to the people suffering from these higher costs. Rural communities in general are struggling as a result of this Budget. In particular, schools are close to their crisis point in too many villages in North Norfolk. Earlier this year, Corpusty primary shut its school gates for the last time. It was heartbreaking for the families affected, and for the children, who were losing the only school that most of them had ever known. We fought tooth and nail against that closure—unlike, I should say, either the Conservative or Reform administrations at County Hall, who stood idly by. I warned anyone who would listen that Corpusty was the canary in the coalmine. Its fundamental challenges were not unique, and it was an indicator of a worrying trend that needs to change. I am deeply fearful of what comes next, because more school leaders and parents are telling me their concerns about their local schools. For all their best efforts, headteachers just cannot make the books balance. It is not their fault; they are being failed by a funding formula that simply does not appreciate the realities of rural life and the importance of rural schools to their communities. In places where there is a fall in the number of children and young people, schools are crying out for a funding package that can help them stay afloat and adapt to a difficult financial and demographic environment. They should feel reassured by the falling rolls funding mechanism, which triggers a £140,000 payout to local authorities through the dedicated schools grant whenever there is a drop of 10%, year on year, in an area’s pupil census. Despite that drop being the reason why that money is coming forward, there is no requirement for it to be spent on those schools, or the issue of falling rolls. It is clear that both sides need to change their processes. The Government need to be more prescriptive about ringfencing, and I will argue that it is not an outlandish ask for falling rolls funding to be dedicated to falling rolls. On their side, the local authority cannot just use this as another sticking plaster to cover educational funding crises. If we do not get a grip on the schools crisis, we face challenging times in our rural communities. If we lose the schools, we lose the working-age population. If we do not fund rural schools properly, whole communities suffer. If there is no local school, the area is not a viable place for a young family to live. That means no one of working age to do the inherently rural jobs in farming, or in the energy industry or defence. In a community without working-age people, there is no one to staff the doctor’s surgery, provide care or even pour a cup of coffee on a Monday morning. We must act now if we want our cherished rural and coastal communities to flourish, and if there is to be good growth in every postcode, there must be cross-governmental support for small rural schools. The Government’s goals—not just for education and economic growth, but for transport, housing, climate change, food security and even defence—all depend on a vibrant future for our rural communities, yet this Budget’s measures are just another example of the Government working in silos, which is not working for our rural areas. It is time to re-establish hope for rural communities by backing small schools.

It is a pleasure to speak in the debate on “fresh hope for the future”, and that title could not be more timely. Across the world, we are living through a period of uncertainty unlike any that many of us have experienced in our lifetime. The challenges we face today are different from those faced by previous generations. Alongside the traditional military threats, we face cyber-attacks, threats to our critical national infrastructure, hostile state activity and economic instability across the globe. In a world like this, national security cannot be an afterthought. In my constituency, we have known that for generations; it is the backbone of the economy and our community. For many of us, defence runs in our blood and in our ancestry, but for too long, communities like mine were asked to believe Conservative promises. We were repeatedly told that defence was the highest priority, yet year after year, we saw programmes delayed, budgets squeezed, and our industry and economy hanging in the balance. That disrupted the lives of my constituents and undermined our national security. The Conservatives claim that they are the party of defence. They stand here today and make more promises that they cannot fulfil. By the time they had left office, the National Audit Office was warning of an “unaffordable equipment programme”. They were running up a bill of tens of billions of pounds that they could not pay. In Barrow, those failed promises have a cost. It impacts investment decisions, training and development opportunities, the supply chain industry and, most critically, confidence for working families that they can put food on the table. That is why this Budget matters. It builds on previous work from the Government to support our national security, and it moves us away from the short-term thinking that characterised the Conservative years. The full funding of the defence investment plan gives industry, workers and communities the confidence that this Government’s commitments are backed by resources, not just rhetoric. Fully funding the DIP sends a powerful message—one that my constituents are well aware of: by investing in defence, we support and empower our communities, our businesses and our national security. Through the defence investment plan, we will deliver stronger military capability, protect our at-sea nuclear deterrent through building up to 12 SSN-AUKUS submarines, and help supply chain businesses all over the country to reach their full potential. We are doing this partly through the innovative defence financing taskforce. For a long time, I have called for a financing and procurement system fit for the modern age. Too many small and medium-sized enterprises are held back by complicated bidding processes, timeline pressures and a risk-averse culture. This taskforce is the first step in addressing those issues. Like many of my colleagues, I firmly believe that it is a priority for us to reach 3% of GDP on defence spending. This is why I was glad to hear the Chancellor confirm last week that the details will be set out at next year’s spending review. This Government are prioritising investment in defence and ensuring that the path to 3% is built on sound financial planning, rather than soundbites. Hope does not only come in the form of long-term investment, though; it also comes through addressing issues that are smaller-scale but no less important. I want to thank the Government for listening on an issue that I recently raised with the Prime Minister. Just two weeks ago, we spoke in this Chamber about my constituent Ian, who requires access to a life-extending medicine. After the June announcement that the application of VAT would be reformed, the drug’s developer withdrew from the scheme through which the drug was provided. Ian was left with no remaining options. With nowhere left to turn, his family were left with an awful choice: find the money to fund the huge cost themselves or, even more unfairly, lose remaining time with their loved one. That is why I welcome the Government’s announcement on VAT and donated medicines.
