Items.Value:
I know that it is unconventional to crowdsource one’s speech on the Budget, but I happened to do my annual online Budget Q&A last night, and it was an absolutely joyful experience. The key themes that were raised with me were: is this Budget bold enough; and what does it do for our communities here in the Cities of London and Westminster? Members will be delighted and perhaps unsurprised to know that the key questions raised by my constituents are very similar to those that are being raised here in the Chamber.

It is really clear to me, as it is to my constituents, that this Government cannot control every challenge beyond our shores, but we can seek stability, strengthen our resilience and support those most in need. The foundations for a more stable economy were established by my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves) when she made the tough choices to stabilise our economy. What we need now is for families to have confidence that they can plan for the future. Businesses need confidence to invest, expand and create jobs, and our economy needs confidence that public finances are being managed responsibly. That is why this Government’s commitment to fiscal discipline and credible fiscal rules is so important.

Economic credibility is not an abstract concept discussed only in this Chamber in Westminster; it affects mortgage rates, investment decisions, business confidence, household budgets and, increasingly, whether people can afford to own a home of their own. That is in stark contrast to the damaging effects of the mini-Budget that the Conservatives want us to forget, but we very much remember it and, sadly, our constituents remember it through their day-to-day budgets. This Government rightly take a responsible approach, and I particularly welcome those measures that are supporting enterprise, investment and job creation. My constituency, the Cities of London and Westminster, has more jobs than people in it, and every day we see the contribution that businesses make to our economy, from small independent firms to globally recognised companies.

Economic security must also include housing security. Far too many people, particularly in London, cannot afford a home of their own. What was particularly important to me in this Budget was the announcement of £432 million of additional investment to stabilise support for the most vulnerable. It was an absolute honour to welcome the Prime Minister and the Chancellor to my constituency on Monday, where we recognised the long-standing work of frontline rough sleeping outreach workers. This was a long-standing call from those who work in the sector to recognise the skilled work they do every single day to help the most vulnerable. I am proud that this Government have made the decision to make long-term investment to keep people off the streets. Not only is it the right decision and the compassionate decision—
Will the hon. Member give way?

I will not give way—we will hopefully move to a vote soon.

This is the right moral decision and the right compassionate decision. It aligns with our values—it should align with everybody’s values—and it is also the right economic decision. It is not in the interests of public spending to allow people to live on the streets. I pay tribute to the work of the Connection at St Martin’s, which hosted us that day.

We have seen the risks that the Opposition are prepared to take with our economy. This Government are taking a responsible approach, which enables us to make those investments in some of the most vulnerable in society. I commend this Budget to the House, and I commend this responsible approach to fiscal discipline, which allows us to make those important political choices.

There is much to welcome in this Budget for my constituents in Hyndburn and Haslingden. Some of the measures include £100 for 41,000 of my residents. They will benefit from this immediate support with their energy bills as we seek to tackle the cost of energy crisis. The measures also include the expansion of paid parental leave to self-employed people, which will help around 90 new families in my patch every single year, and the business rates relief for businesses with rateable values of £18,000 or less, which builds upon and goes further than the previously announced plans to increase business rates relief on pubs from April 2027. I know how hard our pub and shop owners work and the huge contribution they make to our local communities. I must give a shout-out to my local, the White Bull in Oswaldtwistle, which has recently undertaken plans to extend its dining area, and where I would be delighted to treat the Minister to lunch if they were to come and visit—I strongly recommend the Hungarian goulash. I will focus on two main substantive issues in this Budget. First, I welcome the commitment to a mayor of Lancashire. This Labour Government have made it clear that having a mayor is firmly on the table for Lancashire, and at my business event last week, with over 130 leaders from across east Lancashire, business leaders were clear that they want this to happen as quickly as possible. Therefore, it is time for Reform-led Lancashire county council to stop delaying and get behind a mayor for Lancashire, which is key to unlocking our economic potential. But even better, we do not have to wait for a mayor for us to get going. Following the calls from many Labour colleagues, including my hon. Friends the Members for Ribble Valley (Maya Ellis) and for Rossendale and Darwen (Andy MacNae), the Budget includes a commitment to capacity and capability funding for areas that are progressing towards a mayoral strategic authority, which will put £7.7 million of funding into Lancashire from next year. Alongside that, there is the development of the local growth funds, with a total of £80 million for non-mayoral areas to support priority projects that will support their economic growth and development. Secondly, I turn to what this Budget does for entrepreneurs. Some of these measures include the increases to the trading allowance, a proposed young entrepreneurs’ allowance and £200 million of additional funding for female founders. Furthermore, there is a significant set of plans to support early-stage and scale-up funding, with a commitment of an extra £5 billion to the British Business Bank, £450 million of which is allocated to a new venture debt product to help innovative firms access capital without immediate equity dilution. Over the past year, I have been raising with Ministers the challenge faced by these businesses during their pre-commercialisation so-called “valley of death” and the opportunity to help low-carbon technology businesses in Hyndburn and east Lancashire that face this barrier through funding the RedCAT proposals that I have shared. RedCAT provides businesses that are trying to produce new products for their first identified customer, and I hope that through these combined announcements there may be ways of funding RedCAT. I urge Ministers to meet me to work out how we can overcome some of the siloed approaches within Government to unlock this and unlock economic growth not just in Hyndburn and Lancashire, but in other parts of the country. This Budget goes a long way towards helping my constituents through these difficult global headwinds, as well as outlining a broader ambition to reshape our energy markets and the economy for the future in a way that delivers good growth in every postcode and hope in every heart. Devolution is the chance for Lancashire to take control of our own future and stop having to come cap in hand to Westminster. While we work towards this, I will continue to work with Ministers to deliver the jobs, opportunities and growth that Hyndburn desperately needs.

I am the Member of Parliament for Darlington, the home of “No. 11 North” —the Darlington economic campus. I want to put on record my thanks to Beth, Joe, Laura and all the civil servants who worked round the clock to ensure that we could deliver the Chancellor’s first Budget. The Treasury campus in Darlington was the brainchild of the previous Government, and it was funded by this Government to the tune of £118 million for a brand-new hub. It is proof that the best interventions from this place garner cross-party support. I am sure that everyone in this Chamber will agree with investing record amounts in defence to support our world-leading armed forces and defence industry; backing British inventors, innovators and founders, so that if someone has a great idea here, we will make sure they can succeed here; £100 cashback in January for energy bills for 45,000 households in Darlington, and hundreds of thousands more across the country, which is much needed and well received; and hope for our high streets, with a freeze on business rates and an increase in the business rates relief threshold to £18,000, which will benefit 222 business in Darlington. I am particularly pleased to see that these measures are paid for by the global e-marketplaces and by taking the relief from those pesky vape shops. The country and, I am sure, their representatives across the House can all support that. What seems to divide the House is how we should deliver it. It is right that this Government, under this Chancellor, continue their commitment to fiscal responsibility. We must reduce the amount we are paying on debt interest. I welcome the fact that those who have made record profits off the global insecurity that has driven cost of living pressures on households across our country will pay a little bit more through the bank levy. The truth remains that we will not spend more than we earn, but despite record investment, incredible world-leading growth sectors and an army of grafters—yes, in every postcode—we are getting battered by global storms. That is not the fault of the Conservative party, but we feel that the severity of the impact is. I welcome this Budget’s ringfencing of spending on preventive policies and services. Preventive funding should be ringfenced. If the last Government had rediverted the money that they saved through short-term cuts into upgrading the grid, building new nuclear, building new renewables to create energy security, building new hospitals, building council homes—or building any homes—or building roads, building railways or, indeed, investing in our armed forces, perhaps they would still be trusted with an ounce of public money. Instead, they proved to a whole generation that they should not have the keys to Whitehall. They oversaw some of the worst business deals on record, incentivising hotel use by private contractors to house people seeking asylum and outsourcing our pensions, our social care and our post. They failed to prepare for the pandemic, and then they crashed the economy, leading to the fastest annual fall in living standards since records began. Yes, this Government have more to do. I welcome the myriad interventions the Chancellor has made in this Budget aimed at protecting our economy, our industry and our security.

Does my hon. Friend agree that we do not need to choose between cheaper and cleaner energy, as the two can exist in harmony? One of the ways in which that will happen is the abolition of gas standing charges, which will save 23 million homes £45 on average. That is just one of the good things this Labour Government are doing not just to tackle our climate crisis, but to put more money into people’s pockets.

I absolutely agree. The standing charge policy has come up on the doorstep and has really cut through, so I am delighted to see it.

So yes, Darlington is home to “No. 11 North”. Yes, it is home to the world’s first passenger railway, and home to pease pudding, and it is soon to be home to a brand-new multimillion-pound STEM training centre, backed by £16 million from the last Budget, backed by industry and backed by £5 million of Pride in Place funding. Yes, we do have all that, but we are way more than all those things; we are a test case for good growth and we are bucking the national trend. We are a resilient, investable ecosystem. I grew up in a part of Darlington that was historically called Hopetown. We had hope 200 years ago, and we hope again.

Much of the discussion on the Budget has focused on the national level, and rightly so, but for my constituents the true test is whether life in Aylesbury and the villages feels any different—whether decisions in the Budget translate into thriving local businesses, stronger communities and more confidence in our futures. I was out knocking on doors at the weekend, and one lady said to me, “This town is miserable now, isn’t it?”, which always pains me to hear. She said that when she wakes up on a Saturday, she does not head into Aylesbury; instead, she will go over to Tring or Wendover, where she can park cheaply and easily, and find all the shops and cafés she needs. In some ways, she has a point. Over the last decade or two, we have lost many of the shops, pubs and cafés that we used to have, but I know that our town has huge strengths and potential, and this Labour Government’s Budget helps us to start to turn a corner. The fact is that our towns do not thrive by accident. They rely on entrepreneurs who are prepared to take risks, family businesses that have served their communities for generations, and independent retailers that give our town centres their character and identity. These are not simply economic actors; often the same people are sponsoring local sports clubs and community events—I think, for example, of the long partnership between Xpress Labels and Aylesbury United—and they help young people get into work. If we are serious about the future of our high streets, we have to back those businesses to succeed. We have to do that nationally and locally, as Aylesbury town council does very well. I have spoken to many businesses that tell me that business rates remain one of their biggest cost pressures, and the brilliant organisation Buckinghamshire Business First has also raised that issue with me. I welcome the decision to expand small business rates relief and take thousands more local firms out of business rates altogether. Across Buckinghamshire, 2,000 businesses will now be paying no business rates at all. That makes a real difference to small businesses that are trying to invest and take on staff. I also welcome the real-terms freeze in business rates for the next two years for all our retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. I know that the additional 20% relief for pubs, social clubs and most live music venues will be welcomed by many constituents who have written to me about these matters. I welcome the focus in the Budget on support for entrepreneurs and early start-ups. We should be making it easier for people with a business idea to take that first step, which is why the decision to triple the tax-free trading allowance from £1,000 to £3,000 is important. Whether someone is testing a new business idea, turning a hobby into a source of income, or exploring self-employment for the first time, that measure helps to remove barriers and encourages enterprise. I am pleased to see the introduction of the young entrepreneurs allowance, to help young people trying to get into work. I also celebrate further support for female entrepreneurs in the Budget through the new scale-up programme for female founders, and the additional backing from the British Business Bank. We have many brilliant entrepreneurial women in Aylesbury—I think, for example, of Carys Dorritt at The Polka, a digital marketing agency—and we should absolutely be on their side. Helping our businesses to flourish is just one part of the transformation that I want to see in our town centre and on our village high streets. From creating more spaces for young people to improving our green spaces, and from improving public transport to sorting out parking, there is much more to do, but backing businesses that are the beating heart of our towns and villages is a great place to start. If anyone doubts that change is possible, they should take a walk along the High Street opposite Vale Park. For eight years, residents have been campaigning to remove the ugly and dangerous scaffolding that blocked the pavement on the main route into town, and I have been pleased to support them—and finally, last week, we won! You may ask, Madam Deputy Speaker, “What’s the deal with a pile of scaffolding at this late stage in the debate?” Well, what was supposed to be a temporary fix became, over eight years, a sign of how little Buckinghamshire council seemed to care about our town. But it has gone now; we have proved that we can start to change things, and I am hopeful about what is next.
I call the final Back Bencher, Dave Robertson.
Hear, hear!

I am always a little worried when Members cheer because I am last! I join colleagues in recognising and supporting important measures in the Budget that will give people across Lichfield, Burntwood and the villages—the place I call home—valuable breathing space. There are 34,790 households across my constituency that will receive £100 directly into their bank account in January because of this Budget. That comes on top of the removal of VAT from energy bills, the return of the £2 bus fare, and the promise to get rid of standing charges on gas. Haulier businesses have also been supported by the delay to the fuel price escalator. We could go on and on and on. Any of those changes on their own will not be the end of the cost of living crisis, but I am already hearing from people back home who are so happy that this Government understand the importance of giving them that breathing space in their personal finances. The changes to small business rates relief announced by the Chancellor in the Budget will mean that many businesses in our town and city centres and in our villages will be lifted out of paying any business rates at all, and many more will see a smaller bill. Fifteen premises in the centre of Sankey’s Corner in my constituency will be taken out of paying that bill at all—that is a huge number of shops that will now have more money to put back into their businesses and the community. I have been unable to get the total figure for how much will be saved there, but it looks like it will mean an investment into that community of anywhere between £50,000 and £100,000 per year forever. That is a real investment in a high street in Burntwood by this Government. Similarly, of around a dozen shops on the high street in the village of Fradley, four will no longer be paying business rates at all and a further four will have their bills cut because of this Budget. On top of that, across Lichfield and East Staffordshire, some 764 retail, hospitality and leisure businesses will see their rates frozen in cash terms because of decisions made by this Labour Government. I am pleased that the Government are pressing ahead with plans for devolution across Staffordshire and Stoke. While the previous Government pushed power and funding into the West Midlands conurbation and the East Midlands combined authority, they gave a cold shoulder to the county to the north. This Government are prepared to step up and give our county the powers, and drive the economic growth, to bring good jobs across our area. Just yesterday, I spoke to the principal of South Staffordshire college about the importance of getting these powers to where they need to be, so that our skills training can meet the needs of our local area, especially the rural areas of my constituency and the wider county. The economy needs workers, and ensuring that those workers have the skills they need is something that is so important to areas like Staffordshire. I am excited to get the decisions on skills made in the right places. There are a few other points that I wanted to pick up, but in the interests of time I will turn finally to the mineworkers’ pension scheme and the British Coal staff superannuation scheme. The pension schemes for former coalminers and mineworkers have been poorly set up for so long, so I am very pleased that this Government have moved even closer to delivering the justice that coalfield communities—like mine, in Burntwood, Handsacre and the surrounding areas—deserve. The end of the Treasury grabbing half of the scheme surpluses should be applauded; the end of the standstill clause so that bonus pensions can be guaranteed should be applauded; and the previous return of the investment reserve to the people who earned it should be applauded. All those steps for communities should be applauded, and they simply would not have happened without a Labour Government. However, there needs to be action on the last remaining piece of the jigsaw: the final reserve—the guarantor’s fund. The commitment from the Chancellor to move quickly on this, and the commitment this week from the Work and Pensions Secretary this to happen in weeks not months, have been really welcome, but we cannot wait. Miners have already waited for far too long. Every day, miners leave the scheme. Every day, we lose people. We cannot afford to wait any longer. We must push for them, because it is their money—they earned it—and this Labour Government need to do what we should always do: stand up for our mining communities.
I call the shadow Minister.

I thank all right hon. and hon. Members who have taken a part in the debate over the last four days, in particular the more than 40 Members who have spoken in the debate today. If I may, I will mention the contributions made by a few Members on the Conservative and Liberal Democrat Benches. My hon. Friend the Member for Epping Forest (Dr Hudson) talked about the important issue of protecting the green belt. My hon. Friend the Member for Ruislip, Northwood and Pinner (David Simmonds) said that this was one of the most centralising Budgets, despite the rhetoric. The hon. Member for Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross (Jamie Stone) made a beautiful speech about looking for a chair for his wife, and talked about the delivery charges that penalise people in rural areas. My right hon. Friend the Member for Aldridge-Brownhills (Wendy Morton) talked about the importance of business confidence and the fact that it has been in negative territory under this Government for seven months. My hon. Friend the Member for Droitwich and Evesham (Nigel Huddleston) talked about the importance of job losses because of Labour’s decisions and made the absolutely true point that if Labour MPs understood economics, they would not be socialists. The hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller) made an important point about competition for grid connectivity in his constituency, which is a matter of importance across the country. My right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) made a reference to John Lennon, which was a cultural reference about two centuries more modern than I was expecting him to make! We heard a series of excellent speeches from Members on the Conservative Benches and some interesting speeches from Members on the Government Benches, trying to pick through parts of the Budget to talk about. Let me point out the speech by the hon. Member for Erith and Thamesmead (Ms Oppong-Asare), who is also the Chair of a Select Committee. In her speech, she demonstrated what is best about the Select Committee system. Yes, she is a Labour MP, but she stands up for all MPs in the way in which she holds this Government to account. There has been a consistent message from Members on the Conservative Benches: that this Budget has left the British people facing higher inflation, higher interest rates, greater borrowing and more debt than was promised last year—that this Budget will leave families worse off, not better off. May I welcome the Chief Secretary to the Treasury? Here we are—two working people. Did I get that right? This was a Budget of “fiddly” bits, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. It was a “nothing” Budget, according to the CBI. It was “remarkable for its lack of action”, according to the Resolution Foundation. It was, “big in size but small in ambition”, according to the Institute for Government. They are not wrong. The most surprising aspect of this “kick the can down the road” Budget is that the debate managed to last four days. After four days of debate and a week of scrutiny, the abiding sense is that this was a Budget of missed opportunities: a missed opportunity to demonstrate that we are serious about defence; a missed opportunity to get people off welfare and into work; a missed opportunity to spell out the tough decisions needed to curb public spending, eliminate the deficit and cut our debts; and a missed opportunity to support young people wanting to fulfil their potential but finding it hard to get work or worried about their debts. Even the Prime Minister sees this Budget as a missed opportunity, lamenting that it is not “ideal”. I mean, how bad does a Budget have to be for the Prime Minister to disown it before we have even voted on it? Now we have it from Labour MPs themselves: this Budget is as bad as Liz Truss’s Budget—that is true. But the point is that Liz Truss’s period in office was short, sharp and over in a moment. The problem with this Labour Government is that the pain is long, and we are still stuck with it. On defence, my right hon. Friend the Member for Wetherby and Easingwold (Sir Alec Shelbrooke) spoke yesterday of the genuine threat of war. Just days ago, the Government told us to prepare for war in 1,000 days, but at the Budget the Chancellor said that he needed more time to work out how to fund defence. Let us get this straight: the commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence was a matter of principle for the Chancellor in the summer, but, by this Budget, it had become a matter of inconvenience. How can anyone trust his words? The Chancellor says that he has a target for 3%, but he has no commitments and no plans. The Chair of the Defence Committee, the hon. Member for Slough (Mr Dhesi), called that “lamentable”, and he is right. However, in opening the debate on Thursday, the Defence Secretary said that he did not care—that he did not care about the views of the Chair of the Defence Committee. What an arrogant dismissal from a Minister who is barely 15 weeks into the job! No one in this Parliament has a monopoly on wisdom, least of all the Defence Secretary. The OBR says that spending will increase by over £100 billion, to exceed £430 billion by the end of the forecast period, but the Budget contains no plans to bring the ballooning welfare bill under control. The Chancellor seemed confused and a little lost. In his speech last Wednesday, he said: “As the Prime Minister and I have both said, we will bring down the welfare bill, and we will do it in a Labour way.”—[Official Report, 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 311.] The next day on Radio 4, when asked whether the welfare bill would be reduced before the next election, the Chancellor said, “There will be a reduction in the benefits bill. We’ll do that in a Labour way.” That seemed pretty clear, but the Chancellor was then forced to clarify that when he said yes, he really meant to say no. He said that it was “not correct to say that we’re going to bring this welfare bill down in this parliament”, so there we have it—the Labour way to cut welfare is “Yeah, but no, but yeah, but no, but yeah.” As the shadow Business Secretary, my hon. Friend the Member for Hornchurch and Upminster (Julia Lopez), said, it is a “Little Britain” farce from a “Little Britain” Chancellor. As the shadow Chancellor, my hon. Friend the Member for Arundel and South Downs (Andrew Griffith), said on Thursday, the UK Government’s finances are walking along a cliff edge. With our national debt at 100% of GDP and with the Government continuing to tax and borrow more, he was right to do so. You do not help the disadvantaged in our society by dodging hard choices and going broke; you make their lives much harder. A Budget that ignores the warning signals and buries its head in the sand is a Budget that is deliberately increasing the risk to those least able to cope. Rather than cut borrowing, Labour plans to borrow nearly a quarter of a trillion pounds more over just the next two years, costing every British household an extra £476 per year in additional debt interest. That is not smart, and it is not fair—not to this generation, and certainly not to future generations. The Chancellor praised his “fiscal discipline”, but he knows that he is standing on quicksand. Let us be clear: by voting through this Budget, Labour MPs are voting for real-terms cuts to the schools budget, the prisons budget and adult social care—it is there in the documents, in black and white—but they will not vote for real-terms cuts elsewhere. They do not have the backbone for tough decisions. The Chancellor will have to start work on how to raise taxes yet again to fill the £49 billion hole in his finances. The British people should be under no illusion—a fourth tax-raising Labour Budget lies ahead, with massive tax increases to fund Labour’s addiction to borrowing, big government and more welfare. This Budget is not a fair Budget. It raises taxes on savers for being prudent and reducing their dependency on others. It raises taxes on people who rent out their properties so that someone else can have a roof over their head. It snatches away tax relief for people who start a business—not to become a billionaire, but because it is their passion and they want to create a small nest egg for when they retire—and it introduces new taxes at a time when the tax burden is already far too high. A Conservative Government would not shirk their responsibilities to make big decisions. We would take the hard decisions to reduce welfare, improve the productivity of public services and cut back on overseas aid and the size of the civil service, with 50p of every pound saved going to reduce our deficit under our golden economic rule. That is a Conservative plan for governing now, with a team who have deep experience of the world outside politics and a leader with the backbone to see our country through to a more secure, more prosperous and fairer future.

Items.AttributedTo: The Chief Secretary to the Treasury (Emma Reynolds)
Items.Value: This Budget provides breathing space now and fresh hope for the future, which is the focus of today’s debate. I thank all hon. and right hon. Members across this House who have made contributions—not only today, but over the four days of the debate on this Budget—on the action we are taking in government to steer Britain through the global economic storms, kick-start good growth in every postcode, strengthen our national security and chart a new course for our country in the years ahead. Many Members, including my hon. Friends the Members for Barrow and Furness (Michelle Scrogham) and for Rossendale and Darwen (Andy MacNae), rightly stressed the challenges we are facing because of the storms in the global economy. We have heard a lot from Opposition Front Benchers—most of it hot air—but there was not a word of apology for calling on this Government to join the war in the middle east that is driving up energy costs, inflation and the cost of Government borrowing. We cannot wish away these global economic storms. Instead, my right hon. Friend the Chancellor has set out a course to steer this country through them. We have chosen to use some of the fiscal headroom established last year to absorb the impact of the Iran war and to protect the economy, British businesses and family budgets. As my hon. Friends the Members for Cities of London and Westminster (Rachel Blake) and for Darlington (Lola McEvoy) rightly said, fiscal discipline underwrites every policy of this Government. We will meet the fiscal rules in full, and for the first time, in the third year of the forecast. Last year, borrowing fell to its lowest level in six years as a percentage of GDP, and it continues to fall across the forecast. We will not take any lectures from the shadow Chancellor, the hon. Member for Arundel and South Downs (Andrew Griffith) or the shadow Chief Secretary to the Treasury, the hon. Member for North Bedfordshire (Richard Fuller). They like to claim that they were innocent bystanders who just happened to be Treasury Ministers at the time of the Liz Truss mini-Budget. We all know that they were the architects of the mini-Budget. The shadow Chancellor still maintains, and said as recently as September, that there were a “lot of good things” in the mini-Budget, and to this day the British people are paying the price for his failure. Liz Truss’s stint in office might have been short-lived, but the impact was long-lasting. The contrast with this Labour Government could not be clearer. I am proud that the IMF has said that the UK stands out as a country where “action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively”. It has said that we will have the lowest deficit in the G7 by 2029. As my hon. Friend the Member for Macclesfield (Tim Roca) rightly said, the British economy has proven more resilient than many predicted, including Opposition Members. Indeed, it has defied expectations. The Tories and Reform like to talk down our economy, but the fundamentals of the British economy are strong. Public investment is up. Business investment is up to its highest level in 10 years. Productivity has finally turned a corner, and we had the joint-fastest growth in the G7 in the first half of this year.

The Minister talks about people talking down the economy, but the Joseph Rowntree Trust says that Labour is overseeing the sharpest fall in living standards in 65 years. I wonder whether she thinks it is wrong. If she does, how much are the Government overseeing in terms of declining living standards?

The last Parliament was the worst Parliament on record for living standards. Since the last election, living standards have increased by 1.8%. I urge the right hon. Gentleman to read the executive summary from the OBR, which stated:

“As a net importer of energy, the rise in energy prices constitutes a negative terms-of-trade shock for the UK, which pushes up on inflation and lowers real household disposable incomes.”

Those are the global headwinds we are facing.

Following on from my right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes), the Minister will be aware that the Joseph Rowntree Foundation suggests that constituents of mine—families—will be at least £440 worse off in this Parliament. It will be the worst Parliament ever. There is no covid and no new Ukraine impacting on energy prices. Can she answer my right hon. Friend’s question? Is the Joseph Rowntree Foundation wrong or right?

What I say to the right hon. Gentleman is that wages have risen faster in the first two years of this Government than they did in the first 10 years of his Government, so we will take no lectures from him or his party. Against this backdrop, the Chancellor is providing immediate breathing space for families and businesses. Our £100 household energy payment will support 20 million households in England. That is 80% of households, and it will be paid for by a time-limited 3% increase to the bank surcharge, which the Conservatives will oppose in the Lobby. We are going further on bills, by extending the removal of VAT on electricity until July and extending the 5p cut on fuel duty, and next year we will abolish gas standing charges. I thank my hon. Friends the Members for Camborne and Redruth (Perran Moon) and for Bracknell (Peter Swallow), and many others, for welcoming this energy support package. Overall, in 2026-27, households in England are estimated to benefit by about £160 on average from the support that we are providing on energy, according to new analysis published this morning. Households on the lowest incomes are expected to benefit the most, with the bottom 20% benefiting by about £230 on average, almost four times as much as the top 20%. Because we know that higher energy costs are a challenge for business too, we are reducing bills by up to 25% for more than 10,000 eligible businesses from next April through the British industrial competitiveness scheme, as was mentioned by my right hon. Friend the Business Secretary earlier. That will help to support the British firms at the heart of the future of Britain’s reindustrialisation. Beyond energy, we are supporting families by giving self-employed dads paid paternity leave, and I thank my hon. Friends the Members for Reading West and Mid Berkshire (Olivia Bailey) and for Dagenham and Rainham (Margaret Mullane) for welcoming that measure. We are backing British businesses and high streets, and here I would like to correct the record. Of course the brilliant men and women across the country who run small businesses are working people, and I thank them for their contribution to our local economies and our local high streets—the bakeries, the cafés, the restaurants, the beauticians, the hairdressers, the local pubs, and so much more. In the first week of this new Government in July 2024, we cut an extra 20% from business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues from April next year. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith) for her invitation to the pub in her constituency, and I look forward to going there to eat the goulash. In this Budget, the Chancellor has gone further by taking 70,000 more small retail, hospitality and leisure properties out of paying business rates altogether. For all other businesses in those sectors, we are freezing their business rates in real terms. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith)—my constituency neighbour—for what she said about that change in business rates, and the 2,000 small high street businesses across Buckinghamshire, including Aylesbury and indeed High Wycombe, that will be taken out of business rates altogether. To pay for this—as was mentioned by my hon. Friend the Member for Heywood and Middleton North (Mrs Blundell)—we are increasing machine games duty for higher-stakes machines, and we are carving out adult gaming centres and vape shops from business rate reliefs. We are also ensuring that online marketplaces collect and pay VAT, which they should be doing already. Many Members have mentioned young people during the debate. We want young people to have the chance to earn, learn and get on. As the Chancellor has rightly said, we have a moral duty to the next generation. We are raising pay for low-paid workers, while being careful not to price young people out of that crucial first job. We have also expanded access to work experience, and provided record funding for apprenticeships. We have introduced a scheme for first-time buyers, and have capped student loan interest rates at 6%. My hon. Friends the Members for Lichfield (Dave Robertson) and for Merthyr Tydfil and Aberdare (Gerald Jones) mentioned the mineworkers pension scheme. It is this Labour Government who returned the investment fund to the members of the scheme in a previous Budget, and in this Budget the Chancellor has rightly introduced a measure to ensure that not a penny of the surpluses will come back to the Government. Instead, 100% of surpluses will go to the scheme members. As for the outstanding issue of the guarantor’s fund, the Chancellor has made it clear that we will go on to ensure that the full transfer takes place. Resolved,
That—
(1) Schedule 6 to the Finance Act 2000 (climate change levy) is amended as follows.
(2) In paragraph 8(1)(a) (excluded supplies: supply for domestic or charity use), for “paragraph 9” substitute “paragraphs 9 and 9A”.

(a) in sub-paragraph (1), at the end insert—
“Paragraphs (e) and (f) are subject to paragraph 9A.”
(b) in sub-paragraph (2), at the end insert—
“This sub-paragraph does not apply to a supply of electricity which is an electric vehicle charging supply (as to which, see paragraph 9A).”

“Electric vehicle charging supply deemed not to be for domestic use
9A (1) For the purposes of paragraph 8, a supply of electricity is never for domestic use if it is an electric vehicle charging supply.
(2) A supply of electricity is an “electric vehicle charging supply” if the electricity is supplied through an electric vehicle charging point that is—
(a) accessible to the public or a section of the public, or
(b) accessible to employees or contractors at their workplace.
(3) An electric vehicle charging point does not fall within sub-paragraph (2)(a) if it is accessible only to residents of a particular building, or part of a particular building, that—
(a) consists of a dwelling or a number of dwellings, or
(b) is used for a relevant residential purpose.
(4) An electric vehicle charging point is “accessible” if it is accessible (on payment or otherwise)—
(a) as of right, or
(b) by virtue of express or implied permission.
(5) For the purposes of sub-paragraph (3)(b) use for a relevant residential purpose has the same meaning as in paragraph 9(3).
(6) In this paragraph—
“electric vehicle” means a road vehicle that can be propelled by electrical power (whether or not it can also be propelled by another kind of power);
“electric vehicle charging point” means a facility or apparatus for charging an electric vehicle.

(7) The power to make provision under section 29A(3) of the Value Added Tax Act 1994 varying Schedule 7A to that Act (charge at reduced rate) includes power to make provision for any appropriate corresponding variation of this paragraph.”
